newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prosecutors want jail for former spymaster.
newsitem.headline: German prosecutors want jail for former spymaster.

text.p: German prosecutors on Wednesday demanded a three-and-a-half year jail sentence for legendary East German spymaster Markus Wolf, who is charged with three cases of abduction from the 1950s and 1960s.
State prosecutor Joachim Lampe told the state court in Duesseldorf that Wolf had masterminded three abductions and was guilty of intimidation, bodily harm and depriving his victims of their freedom.
Lampe said justice still had to be done, but the prosecutors were demanding a lenient sentence because decades had passed since the crimes were committed.
The suave 73-year-old Wolf, who ran East Berlin's foreign intelligence network for over 30 years, has denied the charges.

Prosecutors last Tuesday dropped charges of treason and extortion against Wolf in order to speed up the trial, their last bid to bring to book the elusive figure dubbed "the man without a face" by his western counterparts, who for decades had little idea what he looked like.

Wolf was convicted of treason in the same Duesseldorf courtroom in 1993. But Germany's highest court overturned the decision in 1995, saying Wolf could not be convicted of spying on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.

This time prosecutors charged Wolf with crimes under East German law, relating to intelligence work in the 1950s and 1960s. Wolf is charged with organising the kidnapping in 1959 of a Ministry for State Security (Stasi) member who had fled to West Germany and the abduction of a West Berlin secretary, who the authorities hoped to persuade to spy for the East.
Prosecutors said Wolf was also behind the arrest of an East German who the Stasi tried to force to take part in a plot against former Chancellor Willy Brandt, then mayor of Berlin.

Wolf ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters. One of his biggest coups was planting "mole" Guenter Guillaume inside Chancellor Brandt's office -- leading to Brandt's resignation in 1974.
